## TL;DR

Mission Control and Stories now use calm, single-column first-load placeholders that do not spill into extra columns at wide widths. The route audit confirms that the remaining skeleton shapes correspond to the data regions those pages render. The app shell owns the 180 ms show delay and 350 ms minimum display time; cached/background data remains visible because the loading shell is only used for the initial repo load, and page-level loaders retain their existing empty-data guards. UI tests cover route mapping, item counts, fast and slow loads, reduced motion, headers, and shell structure. The owner-approved scope removes loading-state screenshots because the capture verifier treats visible loading as a failed shot.

## Work and rationale

Mission Control is a vertically composed dashboard with usage, resource, and status regions; it is not a card board. Its loading shape is therefore one full-width block, with no responsive auto-fit grid. Stories is a list of story rollups and gets one representative row. This keeps the placeholders compact and prevents a fake second row or additional cards appearing at wide, medium, or narrow widths. The page title and description remain static shell chrome above the placeholder.

The route resolver gives each standard route an explicit shape. Work and Inputs use their board column counts from the shared board definitions; the remaining kinds use their declared item counts. The checks mount PageSkeleton for each kind and compare rendered direct items against those definitions. Reduced-motion CSS disables animation, and the skeleton is exposed as a polite status while the enclosing loading region reports `aria-busy`.

| Route / view | Real data layout | Skeleton shape | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `/` Mission Control | Vertically stacked dashboard panels and status regions | One full-width dashboard block | Corrected |
| `/work` | Six status columns | Board columns from `WORK_BOARD_COLUMN_COUNT` | Match |
| `/client-board`, `/inputs` | Three workflow columns | Input board columns from `INPUT_BOARD_COLUMN_COUNT` | Match |
| `/stories` | Vertical story rollup list | One representative row | Corrected |
| `/checks` | Check plan and run tables | Table rows | Match |
| `/releases` | Release summary cards; distribution data list | Cards / table-like placeholder usage | Match |
| `/deployments` | Environment and deployment matrix | Deployment blocks with row matrix | Match |
| `/dev` | Declared run targets | Target cards | Match |
| `/secrets` | Secret key/value rows | Table rows | Match |
| `/agents` | Agent configuration cards | Cards | Match |
| `/settings` | Grouped setting rows | One representative row | Match |
| `/repo` | Repository context documents | One representative row | Match |
| Per-view panels (scheduled tasks, check runs, model providers, reminders) | Empty-state rows or table entries | Rows / table | Minimal and appropriate |

The app shell delays the global skeleton by 180 ms and retains it for at least 350 ms once visible. This policy is centralized in App.vue; individual pages continue to decide whether they have an empty data region to fill. The shell has no cached repo payload to overwrite on initial entry, and background refreshes do not set the initial loading flag again. The shell now uses one computed loading condition and preserves `<RouterView v-else class="main-route" />` so page height and scrolling retain their existing layout contract. The forced Mission Control and Stories loading-shot hook was removed; the skeleton structure and item counts remain covered by component tests.

## Approaches tried

The existing dashboard and Stories mappings were inspected alongside their actual view templates. A multi-card, auto-fit shape was rejected for Mission Control because it falsely suggested repeated cards and could wrap. A full Stories list was also rejected because the task calls for one realistic block, not a fabricated page full of data. Board counts are sourced from the same board status definitions used by the views instead of duplicating those counts in the component.

The shared shell policy was kept at the app boundary rather than adding timing state to every view. Tests use fake timers to exercise the fast-load and minimum-visible cases. An earlier attempt used `loading:dashboard` and `loading:stories` fixtures for review captures; the capture gate correctly rejected them because it saw `aria-busy`. Following the owner's updated scope, I removed those fixture IDs and cleared declared shots with `repoos update 1070 --shots '[]'`.

## Challenges and blockers

The route audit includes routed shell pages and per-view PageSkeleton call sites, which serve different loading scopes. Per-view loaders are guarded by empty-data conditions; they are not shown during populated refreshes. The owner confirmed that handoff-time loading screenshots cannot pass the verifier, so component structure and item-count assertions provide the loading-state evidence; no loading screenshots are declared. A subsequent close-out check caught the App shell's deviation from the `RouterView v-else` layout contract, which is now corrected and covered by the related tests.

No external account, device, or network measurement was needed. No changes were made to the dashboard’s real content or to configuration settings.

## Key learnings

A skeleton should represent the page’s repeated data unit, not its total volume. For a vertical dashboard or feed, a single broad block or representative row communicates loading without inventing extra content. Shared constants prevent board skeletons from drifting when columns change. Loading timing is most predictable when the shell owns it once, while each view retains its existing knowledge of whether cached or already-loaded data makes a placeholder unnecessary.
